bricks.title: Regional Anatomy of the Posterior Abdominal Wall, Back, and Posterior Neck

items.why: PAW skeletal framework: lumbar vertebrae, 12th rib, pelvis, proximal femur

questions.q: The iliopsoas runs from the lumbar vertebrae and iliac fossa to which attachment?
questions.explain: The iliopsoas extends from the lumbar vertebrae and iliac fossa to the lesser trochanter of the femur.

items.excerpt: The posterior abdominal wall is supported by the lumbar vertebrae, twelfth rib, pelvis, and proximal femur.

items.why: Iliopsoas: primary hip flexor; psoas L1-L3 anterior rami, iliacus femoral n.; psoas abscess/hematoma

questions.q: Which muscle of the posterior abdominal wall is the primary flexor of the hip?
questions.explain: The iliopsoas (psoas major and iliacus) is the primary hip flexor; quadratus lumborum stabilizes the 12th rib and laterally flexes the spine.

questions.q: Which nerve innervates the iliacus?
questions.explain: The iliacus is supplied by the femoral nerve (L2-L4), whereas psoas major is supplied directly by anterior rami of L1-L3.

questions.q: A patient with tuberculous spondylitis (Pott disease) develops fever, back pain, and holds the hip slightly flexed. Infection has most likely spread into which compartment?
questions.explain: In Pott disease, vertebral infection can spread into the psoas compartment, producing a psoas abscess; patients hold the hip flexed to avoid stretching the muscle.

items.excerpt: Extending from the lumbar vertebrae and iliac fossa to the lesser trochanter of the femur, it is the primary flexor of the hip…

items.why: Quadratus lumborum: iliac crest to 12th rib/lumbar TPs; stabilizes 12th rib, ipsilateral lateral flexion; T12-L4

questions.q: What is the primary action of the quadratus lumborum?
choices: Ipsilateral lateral flexion of the spine
questions.explain: Quadratus lumborum stabilizes (fixes) the 12th rib during respiration and produces ipsilateral lateral flexion of the vertebral column.

questions.q: The quadratus lumborum is innervated by which nerves?
questions.explain: Like the other posterior abdominal wall muscles, quadratus lumborum is supplied by anterior rami (T12-L4).

items.excerpt: It stabilizes the twelfth rib during respiration and produces ipsilateral lateral flexion of the vertebral column.

items.why: Trapezius: CN XI motor; transverse cervical a.; elevates, retracts, depresses, upwardly rotates scapula

questions.q: Which nerve provides motor innervation to the trapezius?
questions.explain: The trapezius is the exception among extrinsic back muscles: motor supply is CN XI, with C3-C4 carrying sensory/proprioceptive fibers.

questions.q: Which artery is the main blood supply of the trapezius?
questions.explain: Table 3 lists the transverse cervical artery as the blood supply of the trapezius.

items.excerpt: The trapezius is an exception, receiving motor innervation from the spinal accessory nerve (CN XI).

items.why: Latissimus dorsi: thoracodorsal n. and a.; extends, adducts, medially rotates arm

questions.q: Which nerve innervates the latissimus dorsi?
questions.explain: Latissimus dorsi is supplied by the thoracodorsal nerve and thoracodorsal artery.

questions.q: Which set of arm movements does the latissimus dorsi produce?
questions.explain: Latissimus dorsi extends, adducts, and medially rotates the arm (e.g., climbing and pulling).

items.excerpt: Latissimus dorsi: Thoracodorsal nerve; Thoracodorsal artery; Extends, adducts, and medially rotates the arm

items.why: Levator scapulae: dorsal scapular n./a.; elevates scapula

questions.q: Which nerve innervates the levator scapulae?
questions.explain: Levator scapulae is supplied by the dorsal scapular nerve and artery and elevates the scapula.

items.excerpt: Levator scapulae: Dorsal scapular nerve; Dorsal scapular artery; Elevates the scapula

items.why: Rhomboid major: dorsal scapular n.; retracts and stabilizes scapula

questions.q: What is the primary action of rhomboid major?
questions.explain: Rhomboid major and minor retract and stabilize the scapula; they are supplied by the dorsal scapular nerve.

items.excerpt: Rhomboid major & minor: Dorsal scapular nerve; Dorsal scapular artery; Retracts and stabilizes the scapula

items.why: Rhomboid minor: dorsal scapular n./a.; retracts scapula

questions.q: Which artery supplies rhomboid minor?
questions.explain: Both rhomboids (and levator scapulae) are supplied by the dorsal scapular nerve and dorsal scapular artery.

items.excerpt: The superficial extrinsic back muscles include the trapezius, latissimus dorsi, levator scapulae, and rhomboid major and minor

items.why: Serratus posterior sup/inf: intermediate extrinsic; intercostal nn.; mainly proprioceptive

questions.q: Although classed as accessory respiratory muscles, the serratus posterior muscles are thought to function mainly in what?
questions.explain: The serratus posterior superior and inferior play only a minor role in breathing and are thought to contribute primarily to proprioception.

questions.q: Serratus posterior inferior is innervated by which nerves?
questions.explain: Serratus posterior superior is supplied by intercostal nerves T2-T5 and serratus posterior inferior by T9-T12.

items.excerpt: …they play only a minor role in breathing and are thought to contribute primarily to proprioception.

items.why: Anterior rami: supply extrinsic back and posterior abdominal wall muscles

questions.q: The extrinsic back muscles (except trapezius) are innervated primarily by which branches?
questions.explain: Extrinsic back muscles are supplied mainly by anterior rami, reflecting their embryologic link with limb musculature.

items.excerpt: …they are innervated primarily by anterior rami of spinal nerves, reflecting their embryologic association with the limb musculature.

items.why: Typical vertebra: body anterior, vertebral arch posterior (pedicles + laminae)

questions.q: The vertebral arch of a typical vertebra is formed by which paired parts?
questions.explain: A typical vertebra has a body anteriorly and a vertebral arch posteriorly formed by paired pedicles and laminae.

items.excerpt: A typical vertebra consists of a body anteriorly and a vertebral arch posteriorly.

items.why: Pedicle: part of arch; vertebral notches of adjacent pedicles form intervertebral foramen

questions.q: The superior and inferior vertebral notches of adjacent pedicles form which opening?
questions.explain: Each intervertebral foramen is formed in part by the vertebral notches of adjacent pedicles; spinal nerves exit through it.

items.excerpt: Each intervertebral foramen is formed in part by the superior and inferior vertebral notches of adjacent pedicles.

items.why: Lamina: posterior part of arch between transverse and spinous processes

questions.q: Which part of a vertebra forms the posterior arch between the transverse and spinous processes?
questions.explain: The laminae form the posterior portion of the vertebral arch, between the transverse process and the spinous process.

items.excerpt: Which part of a typical vertebra forms the posterior portion of the vertebral arch between the transverse process and spinous process?

items.why: Vertebral foramen: surrounded by body + arch; stacked foramina form vertebral canal

questions.q: Successive vertebral foramina together form what structure?
questions.explain: The body and arch surround the vertebral foramen; the vertebral foramina of successive vertebrae form the vertebral canal.

items.excerpt: The vertebral arch is formed by paired pedicles and laminae and, together with the body, surrounds the vertebral foramen.

items.why: Vertebral canal: formed by stacked vertebral foramina; houses the spinal cord
items.excerpt: The vertebral foramina of successive vertebrae collectively form the vertebral canal.

items.why: Spinous process: back muscle/ligament attachment; C7 vertebra prominens is a palpable landmark

questions.q: Which spinous process is usually easily palpable at the base of the neck and used to count vertebral levels?
questions.explain: The spinous process of C7 (vertebra prominens) is a key palpable landmark at the base of the neck.

items.excerpt: The spinous process of C7 (vertebra prominens) is usually easily palpable at the base of the neck…

items.why: Transverse process: attachment site; QL attaches to TPs of upper lumbar vertebrae

questions.q: The quadratus lumborum attaches superiorly to the twelfth rib and to which vertebral feature?
choices: Spinous processes of upper lumbar vertebrae
Transverse processes of upper lumbar vertebrae
Bodies of the lower thoracic vertebrae
Laminae of the lower lumbar vertebrae
questions.explain: Quadratus lumborum runs from the iliac crest and iliolumbar ligament to the 12th rib and the transverse processes of the upper lumbar vertebrae.

items.excerpt: The spinous and transverse processes provide important attachment sites for the muscles and ligaments of the back.

items.why: Intervertebral foramen: spinal nerves exit the vertebral canal

questions.q: What passes through the intervertebral foramina?
questions.explain: Spinal nerves exit the vertebral canal through the intervertebral foramina, which lie between adjacent vertebrae.

items.excerpt: The intervertebral foramina are openings between adjacent vertebrae through which spinal nerves exit the vertebral canal.

items.why: Cervical vertebra: identified by transverse foramina

questions.q: Which feature is characteristic of cervical vertebrae?
questions.explain: Cervical vertebrae have transverse foramina; thoracic vertebrae have rib facets; lumbar vertebrae have large bodies.

items.excerpt: Cervical vertebrae are characterized by transverse foramina.

items.why: Transverse foramen: transmits the vertebral artery, usually entering at C6

questions.q: At which level does the vertebral artery typically enter the transverse foramina?
questions.explain: The vertebral arteries typically enter the transverse foramina at C6 and ascend to the atlas before entering the skull through the foramen magnum.

items.excerpt: The vertebral arteries ascend through the transverse foramina of the cervical vertebrae, typically entering at the level of C6…

items.why: Vertebral artery: ascends in transverse foramina, enters skull via foramen magnum; compression -> vertigo, ataxia

questions.q: Osteophytes and extreme neck rotation compress a vertebral artery. Which presentation is most expected?
choices: Wrist drop and dorsal hand numbness
questions.explain: Vertebral artery compression reduces flow to the brainstem, cerebellum, and occipital lobes, causing dizziness, vertigo, ataxia, visual disturbances, or syncope.

questions.q: The vertebral artery enters the cranial cavity through which opening?
questions.explain: After ascending through the cervical transverse foramina to C1, the vertebral artery enters the cranial cavity through the foramen magnum.

items.excerpt: …can injure or compress a vertebral artery, reducing blood flow to the brainstem, cerebellum, and occipital lobes.

items.why: Thoracic vertebra: facets for rib articulation

questions.q: Which feature distinguishes thoracic vertebrae?
questions.explain: Thoracic vertebrae have costal facets for articulation with the ribs.

items.excerpt: Thoracic vertebrae have facets for articulation with the ribs.

items.why: Costal facets: rib articulations on thoracic vertebrae
items.excerpt: Thoracic vertebrae have facets for articulation with the ribs.

items.why: Lumbar vertebra: large bodies to bear greater weight

questions.q: Why are lumbar vertebral bodies so large?
choices: To allow rotation of the head
questions.explain: Lumbar vertebrae have large vertebral bodies adapted to support greater weight.

items.excerpt: Lumbar vertebrae have large vertebral bodies adapted to support greater weight.

items.why: Atlas (C1): no body or typical spinous process; atlanto-occipital joint with occipital condyles

questions.q: Which vertebra lacks a body and articulates with the occipital condyles?
questions.explain: The atlas lacks a body and a typical spinous process and articulates with the occipital condyles at the atlanto-occipital joints.

items.excerpt: The atlas (C1) lacks a body and a typical spinous process and articulates superiorly with the occipital condyles at the atlanto-occipital joints.

items.why: Axis (C2) and dens: pivot for head rotation at the atlantoaxial joint

questions.q: The dens of the axis is the pivot for which movement?
questions.explain: The dens projects superiorly and is the pivot around which the atlas and head rotate at the atlantoaxial joint.

items.excerpt: The axis (C2) is distinguished by the dens, which projects superiorly and provides a pivot around which the atlas and head rotate…

items.why: Posterior rami: innervate all intrinsic back muscles

questions.q: Intrinsic back muscles such as the erector spinae and multifidus are supplied by which branches?
questions.explain: The intrinsic back muscles are innervated by posterior (dorsal) rami of spinal nerves.

items.excerpt: They primarily move and stabilize the vertebral column and head and are innervated by the posterior (dorsal) rami of spinal nerves.

items.why: Splenius capitis/cervicis: most superficial intrinsic layer of neck; ipsilateral rotation; cervical posterior rami

questions.q: Acting unilaterally, the splenius muscles rotate the head in which way?
questions.explain: Bilaterally the splenius capitis and cervicis extend the head and neck; unilaterally they laterally flex and rotate it to the same side.

questions.q: The splenius muscles are innervated by which nerves?
questions.explain: As intrinsic back muscles, the splenius muscles are supplied by posterior (dorsal) rami of cervical spinal nerves.

items.excerpt: The splenius capitis and splenius cervicis form the most superficial layer of the intrinsic back muscles in the posterior neck

items.why: Erector spinae (iliocostalis, longissimus, spinalis): largest intrinsic group; extends spine, posture; posterior rami

questions.q: A 68-year-old man has weak vertebral column extension and trouble maintaining upright posture, with normal scapular movement. Which muscle group is most likely affected?
questions.explain: The erector spinae is the largest intrinsic back group; it extends and laterally flexes the spine and maintains upright posture.

questions.q: Which nerves innervate the erector spinae?
questions.explain: All intrinsic back muscles, including the erector spinae, are supplied by posterior (dorsal) rami.

items.excerpt: The erector spinae is the largest intrinsic back muscle group and consists of the iliocostalis, longissimus, and spinalis muscles

items.why: Transversospinalis (semispinalis, multifidus, rotatores): deep to erector spinae; stabilizes, contralateral rotation

questions.q: Which intrinsic back group lies deep to the erector spinae and assists contralateral rotation of the spine?
questions.explain: The transversospinalis group sits in the groove between transverse and spinous processes, stabilizes adjacent vertebrae, and assists extension and contralateral rotation.

items.excerpt: These muscles stabilize adjacent vertebrae and assist with extension and contralateral rotation of the vertebral column.

items.why: Semispinalis: transversospinalis muscle; suboccipital muscles lie beneath semispinalis capitis

questions.q: The suboccipital muscles lie directly deep to which muscle?
questions.explain: The suboccipital muscles lie deep in the posterior neck beneath the semispinalis capitis, a transversospinalis muscle.

items.excerpt: These muscles lie deep in the posterior neck beneath the semispinalis capitis.

items.why: Multifidus: transversospinalis; key stabilizer of lumbar spine; implicated in mechanical LBP

questions.q: Which transversospinalis muscle is particularly important for stabilizing the lumbar spine?
questions.explain: The multifidus is particularly important for lumbar stability; its weakness contributes to mechanical low back pain.

items.excerpt: The multifidus is particularly important for stabilizing the lumbar spine during movement.

items.why: Suboccipital triangle: RCP major + obliquus sup/inf; contains vertebral a. and suboccipital n.

questions.q: Which structures lie within the suboccipital triangle?
choices: Deep cervical artery and C2 root
questions.explain: The triangle bounded by rectus capitis posterior major and obliquus capitis superior and inferior contains the vertebral artery and suboccipital nerve.

questions.q: The suboccipital muscles are innervated by which nerve?
questions.explain: The suboccipital nerve is the posterior ramus of C1; these muscles fine-tune movement at the atlanto-occipital and atlantoaxial joints.

items.excerpt: …3 muscles bounding the suboccipital triangle containing the vertebral artery and suboccipital nerve

items.why: SCM: manubrium/clavicle to mastoid; CN XI; unilateral contralateral rotation; torticollis

questions.q: Acting unilaterally, the sternocleidomastoid turns the head in which way?
questions.explain: Unilaterally the SCM laterally flexes the neck and rotates the head to the opposite side; bilaterally it flexes the neck.

questions.q: An infant's head is tilted toward the left with the chin rotated to the right because of fibrosis of a neck muscle. Which condition is this?
questions.explain: Torticollis is shortening of the SCM, tilting the head toward the affected side and rotating it away; it is often treated with stretching in infancy.

questions.q: Which nerve provides motor innervation to the sternocleidomastoid?
questions.explain: Like the trapezius, the SCM receives motor innervation from CN XI; C2-C3 carry sensory/proprioceptive fibers.

items.excerpt: Acting unilaterally, it laterally flexes the neck and rotates the head to the opposite side.

items.why: Mastoid process: superior attachment of SCM

questions.q: Which muscle attaches to the mastoid process of the temporal bone?
questions.explain: The sternocleidomastoid extends from the manubrium and clavicle to the mastoid process.

items.excerpt: The sternocleidomastoid … extends from the manubrium and clavicle to the mastoid process of the temporal bone.

items.why: Posterior triangle: SCM is anterior boundary; contains CN XI, brachial plexus roots, EJV

questions.q: Which muscle forms the anterior boundary of the posterior triangle of the neck?
questions.explain: The SCM is the anterior boundary of the posterior triangle, which contains CN XI, roots of the brachial plexus, and the external jugular vein.

questions.q: Which of these lies in the posterior triangle of the neck?
questions.explain: The posterior triangle contains the spinal accessory nerve, the roots of the brachial plexus, and the external jugular vein.

items.excerpt: It is the anterior boundary of the posterior triangle, where the spinal accessory nerve, roots of the brachial plexus, and the external jugular vein…

items.why: Manubrium: inferior (sternal) attachment of SCM
items.excerpt: The sternocleidomastoid … extends from the manubrium and clavicle to the mastoid process of the temporal bone.

items.why: Clavicle: inferior (clavicular) attachment of SCM
items.excerpt: The sternocleidomastoid … extends from the manubrium and clavicle to the mastoid process of the temporal bone.

groups.title: Skeletal Framework of the Vertebral Column

items.why: Spinal cord regions: 31 pairs (C8, T12, L5, S5, Co1); C1-C7 exit above, others below their vertebrae

questions.q: How many pairs of spinal nerves arise from the cervical spinal cord?
questions.explain: There are 8 cervical nerve pairs but only 7 cervical vertebrae; in total there are 31 pairs of spinal nerves.

questions.q: Which spinal nerve exits above the T1 vertebra?
questions.explain: C1-C7 exit above their vertebrae; there is no C8 vertebra, so C8 exits above T1 and thoracic and lower nerves exit below their vertebrae.

items.excerpt: There are 31 pairs of spinal nerves grouped into five regions: cervical, thoracic, lumbar, sacral, and coccygeal

items.why: Posterior root: sensory fibers enter; cell bodies in dorsal root ganglia

questions.q: Where are the cell bodies of the sensory fibers in the posterior (dorsal) root?
questions.explain: Sensory fibers enter through the posterior roots; their primary sensory neuron cell bodies lie in the dorsal root ganglia.

items.excerpt: At each segment, sensory fibers enter the spinal cord through the posterior (dorsal) roots, while motor fibers leave through the anterior (ventral) roots.

items.why: Anterior root: motor fibers (somatic and preganglionic autonomic) leave the cord

questions.q: Axons of ventral horn somatic motor neurons leave the spinal cord through which structure?
questions.explain: Motor fibers, including preganglionic autonomic axons from the lateral horn, leave the cord through the anterior roots.

items.excerpt: Axons from these autonomic motor neurons leave the spinal cord through the ventral roots before traveling to autonomic ganglia.

items.why: Spinal nerve: mixed nerve formed by posterior + anterior roots; exits via intervertebral foramen

questions.q: Which statement best describes a spinal nerve?
choices: Mixed nerve formed by both roots
Purely sensory branch of the cord
Purely motor branch of the cord
questions.explain: The posterior and anterior roots join to form a mixed spinal nerve, which leaves through the intervertebral foramen and splits into rami.

items.excerpt: The posterior and anterior roots join to form a mixed spinal nerve that connects the spinal cord with the periphery…

items.why: Posterior ramus: mixed primary ramus of the spinal nerve
items.excerpt: …connects the spinal cord with the periphery through mixed dorsal (posterior) and ventral (anterior) primary rami.

items.why: Anterior ramus: mixed primary ramus of the spinal nerve
items.excerpt: …are distributed through the dorsal and ventral primary rami to innervate skeletal muscles of the back, trunk, and limbs

items.why: Conus medullaris: tapered end of cord at about L1-L2 in adults

questions.q: In adults, the spinal cord tapers into the conus medullaris at about which vertebral level?
questions.explain: In adults the cord extends from the foramen magnum to about L1-L2, where it ends as the conus medullaris.

items.excerpt: In adults, the spinal cord extends from the foramen magnum to approximately the L1–L2 vertebral level, where it tapers to form the conus medullaris.

items.why: Cauda equina: lumbar, sacral, coccygeal roots descending below the conus

questions.q: Why do lower spinal nerve roots descend within the vertebral canal as the cauda equina?
choices: The roots must pass through the dura
The cord ends at the coccyx in adults
The vertebral column outgrows the cord
The roots join the brachial plexus
questions.explain: Because the vertebral column grows faster than the cord, lumbar, sacral, and coccygeal roots descend before exiting, forming the cauda equina.

items.excerpt: In adults, the spinal cord typically ends at the L1-L2 vertebral level as the conus medullaris; spinal nerve roots continuing inferiorly form the cauda equina.

items.why: Dura mater: outermost meninx; puncture -> CSF leak, post-dural puncture headache

questions.q: What is the correct order of the spinal meninges from superficial to deep?
questions.explain: The dura mater is most external, the arachnoid mater is the middle layer, and the pia mater is most internal.

questions.q: During epidural anesthesia, accidental puncture of the dura mater most likely causes which complication?
questions.explain: Puncturing the dura can let CSF leak, producing a post-dural puncture headache.

items.excerpt: Accidental puncture of the dura mater may result in leakage of cerebrospinal fluid and a post-dural puncture headache.

items.why: Arachnoid mater: middle meninx; subarachnoid space lies deep to it

questions.q: CSF lies between the arachnoid mater and which other layer?
questions.explain: The subarachnoid space, between the arachnoid and pia mater, contains cerebrospinal fluid.

items.excerpt: Between the arachnoid and pia mater is the subarachnoid space, which contains cerebrospinal fluid (CSF).

items.why: Pia mater: innermost meninx, directly on the cord
items.excerpt: The meninges are composed of three layers … Pia mater (most internal)

items.why: Epidural space: real space with fat, vessels, lymphatics; site of epidural anesthesia

questions.q: Epidural anesthetic for labor is injected into a space containing which contents?
questions.explain: The spinal epidural space, outside the dura, contains epidural fat, blood vessels, and lymphatics; anesthetic there bathes the spinal nerve roots.

questions.q: How does the spinal epidural space differ from the cranial epidural space?
choices: Spinal is a real space; cranial is potential
Spinal is potential; cranial is a real space
Both are filled with cerebrospinal fluid
Both lie between arachnoid and pia
questions.explain: In the vertebral canal the epidural space is an actual space filled with fat; around the brain it is only a potential space between skull and dura.

items.excerpt: Within the vertebral column, the epidural space of the spinal cord is an actual space occupied by the epidural fat.

items.why: Subarachnoid space: between arachnoid and pia; contains CSF

questions.q: Which space contains cerebrospinal fluid?
questions.explain: The subarachnoid space, between the arachnoid and pia mater, contains CSF.

items.excerpt: The subarachnoid space, between the arachnoid mater and pia mater, contains cerebrospinal fluid.

items.why: Lumbar cistern: enlarged subarachnoid space below conus; LP at L3-L4/L4-L5

questions.q: A lumbar puncture is commonly performed between which vertebrae?
questions.explain: Because the cord ends at L1-L2, the needle is placed at L3-L4 or L4-L5 into the lumbar cistern, where cauda equina roots float in CSF.

questions.q: During a lumbar puncture, which ligament is the last one pierced before the vertebral canal is entered?
questions.explain: The needle passes the supraspinous ligament, then the interspinous ligament, then the ligamentum flavum before entering the vertebral canal.

items.excerpt: Inferior to the conus medullaris, the subarachnoid space enlarges to form the lumbar cistern, which contains CSF and the nerve roots of the cauda equina.

items.why: Vertebral canal: houses the spinal cord
items.excerpt: The spinal cord is a tubular structure of nervous tissue that … extends caudally within the vertebral canal.

items.why: Vertebral foramina stack to form the vertebral canal
items.excerpt: As described in the regional anatomy of the back, successive vertebral foramina form the vertebral canal.

items.why: Intervertebral foramina: exit of spinal nerves
items.excerpt: Spinal nerve roots extend from the spinal cord and join to form spinal nerves, which leave the vertebral column through the intervertebral foramina

bricks.title: Functional Anatomy of the Shoulder & Arm

items.why: Clavicle: strut holding limb from thorax; SC joint medially, AC joint laterally

questions.q: What is the main mechanical role of the clavicle?
choices: A socket for the head of the humerus
A strut holding the limb off the thorax
Origin of the rotator cuff muscles
Attachment of the long head of biceps
questions.explain: The clavicle acts as a strut that holds the upper limb away from the thoracic wall, articulating with the sternum medially and the acromion laterally.

items.excerpt: The clavicle acts as a strut that holds the upper limb away from the thoracic wall, allowing greater freedom of movement.

items.why: Sternum: medial articulation of the clavicle (SC joint)
items.excerpt: Medially, it articulates with the sternum at the sternoclavicular joint.

items.why: Scapula: flat triangular bone on the posterior thoracic wall
items.excerpt: The scapula is a flat triangular bone located on the posterior thoracic wall.

items.why: Spine of scapula: divides posterior surface into supra/infraspinous fossae; expands as acromion

questions.q: The spine of the scapula expands laterally to form which feature?
questions.explain: The scapular spine divides the posterior surface into the supraspinous and infraspinous fossae and expands laterally as the acromion.

items.excerpt: The spine of the scapula divides its posterior surface into supraspinous and infraspinous fossae.

items.why: Supraspinous fossa: home of supraspinatus, which initiates abduction

questions.q: The muscle filling the supraspinous fossa is innervated by which nerve?
questions.explain: Supraspinatus (in the supraspinous fossa) initiates abduction and is supplied by the suprascapular nerve.

items.excerpt: The spine of the scapula divides its posterior surface into supraspinous and infraspinous fossae.

items.why: Infraspinous fossa: home of infraspinatus (lateral rotation, suprascapular n.)

questions.q: The muscle filling the infraspinous fossa mainly produces which movement?
questions.explain: Infraspinatus, in the infraspinous fossa, laterally rotates the humerus and is supplied by the suprascapular nerve.

items.excerpt: The spine of the scapula divides its posterior surface into supraspinous and infraspinous fossae.

items.why: Acromion: forms AC joint; supraspinatus tendon passes beneath it (impingement)

questions.q: Which tendon passes beneath the acromion and is most often torn in rotator cuff injury?
questions.explain: The supraspinatus tendon passes beneath the acromion and coracoacromial arch to the greater tubercle, making it vulnerable to impingement and tears.

items.excerpt: The supraspinatus tendon passes beneath the acromion before inserting on the greater tubercle of the humerus.

items.why: Coracoid process: origin of short head of biceps and coracobrachialis; part of CA arch

questions.q: Which muscle arises from the coracoid process?
questions.explain: The short head of biceps and the coracobrachialis arise from the coracoid process; the long head of biceps arises from the supraglenoid tubercle.

items.excerpt: The coracoid process projects anteriorly and serves as an attachment site for several muscles and ligaments.

items.why: Glenoid cavity: articulates with humeral head to form GH joint

questions.q: The glenoid cavity articulates with which structure?
questions.explain: The glenoid cavity articulates with the head of the humerus to form the glenohumeral joint.

items.excerpt: The glenoid cavity articulates with the head of the humerus to form the glenohumeral joint.

items.why: Suprascapular n.: under superior transverse scapular ligament ('Navy under the bridge')

questions.q: At the suprascapular notch, how does the suprascapular nerve relate to the superior transverse scapular ligament?
choices: It runs lateral to the notch
questions.explain: 'Army over the bridge, Navy under': the artery passes above the ligament and the nerve passes beneath it.

items.excerpt: The suprascapular notch … transmits the suprascapular nerve beneath the superior transverse scapular ligament, while the suprascapular artery passes above the ligament.

items.why: Humerus: single long bone of the arm
items.excerpt: The arm extends from the shoulder to the elbow and contains a single long bone, the humerus.

items.why: Head of humerus: articulates with glenoid cavity
items.excerpt: The glenohumeral joint is a ball and socket synovial joint formed by the head of the humerus and the glenoid cavity of the scapula.

items.why: Anatomical neck: part of the proximal humerus
items.excerpt: The proximal humerus includes the head, anatomical neck, greater and lesser tubercles, intertubercular groove, and surgical neck.

questions.explain: Lumbricals and interossei flex the metacarpophalangeal joints while extending the interphalangeal joints.

items.excerpt: Together, they flex the metacarpophalangeal joints while extending the interphalangeal joints, allowing the fingers to conform to objects of different shapes.

items.why: IP joints: FDS flexes PIP, FDP flexes DIP; claw = IP flexion

questions.q: In an ulnar claw deformity, what is the position of the interphalangeal joints of digits 4 and 5?
questions.explain: Ulnar claw shows MCP hyperextension with IP flexion, most marked in digits 4 and 5.
